Q: How to reliably locate elements in Playwright when id, class, and name attributes are missing or dynamic? A:

There is no universal method.

Sometimes element may have other unique attribute - data-*, aria-*, text (or some part of text).

Sometimes even dynamic id, name, class may have some part stable and unique. [contains(@class, 'hello')]

Sometimes element has unique parent(s) - div.unique > a > img, div[@class="unique"]/a/img.

Or it has always the same position in HTML and you can use index - e.g. first <tr> in second <table> - (//table)[2]//tr[1]

Q: How to create a vector where each number doubles the last number? A:

You can use bitwShiftL, which gives the desired output and runs fast as well

> library(microbenchmark)
> n <- 0:20
> f1 <- \(n) 2^n
> f2 <- \(n) bitwShiftL(1,n)
> microbenchmark(f1 = f1(n), f2 = f2(n), unit = "relative", check = "equivalent")
Unit: relative
 expr min       lq      mean   median       uq        max neval
   f1 2.4 2.166667 0.1756371 2.166667 2.333333 0.01051552   100
   f2 1.0 1.000000 1.0000000 1.000000 1.000000 1.00000000   100

Q: TortoiseGit, ignore line endings A:

We may all have different versions of TortoiseGit, because in the answer from Yue Lin Ho the screenshot of Settings didn't match for me. (I'm on version TortoiseGit 2.11.0.0 in a VMWare Virtual Machine.) It did still help me get started though, and I figured out what worked for me:

Right click in on any file or folder in the repository -> TortoiseGit -> Settings. Set AutoCrLf and SafeCrLf to true in their drop-down boxes (I did this for Local, Global, and System (sorry, I don't know what the difference is between those) as seen in the yellow highlighted box below:

Be sure to click Apply before switching between Local, Global, and System, though, because the settings won't save without clicking Apply between scopes.

Now, gloriously, all hundreds of newline differenced files do not show in the diff window.

Q: How could I specifically get the name of a window that I want to focus and not have to sort through them oddly? A:

The issue you're running into isn't actually a problem with PyWin32; it's a quirk of how the underlying Windows API function, EnumWindows, behaves.

In Windows, almost every UI element—buttons, text fields, menus, dropdowns, and radio buttons—is technically considered a "window" and is assigned its own hWnd. When developers create these child controls using CreateWindowW or CreateWindowExW, they are supposed to bind them to a parent window using the hWndParent parameter.

If they fail to do that (which is incredibly common), EnumWindows will treat those orphaned buttons and text fields as top-level windows and return them. Because of this, EnumWindows usually gets flooded with invisible "junk" handles, making it far too unreliable for just finding basic application windows.

A much cleaner alternative is pyvda. It uses COM interfaces designed specifically for managing virtual desktops. Because of this, it naturally filters out the clutter and only returns the hWnds of the actual, visible parent windows that you see on your screen.

The following class will return any parent window that is attached to a 'Spotify' executable. I've also stripped the need for PyWin32, and used Python's builtin ctypes for accessing the Windows API.

import ctypes
from ctypes import wintypes

from psutil import Process
from pyvda import AppView
from pyvda.com_defns import IApplicationView
from pyvda.utils import Managers


class AppProcess(Process, AppView):
    __MANAGERS = Managers()

    @property
    def caption(self) -> str:
        text_len = self.__GetWindowTextLength(self.hwnd) + 1
        text_buffer = ctypes.create_unicode_buffer(text_len)

        self.__GetWindowText(self.hwnd, text_buffer, text_len)
        return text_buffer.value

    def __init__(self, view: IApplicationView):
        self.__init_win32_api_function_prototypes()

        AppView.__init__(self, view = view)
        Process.__init__(self, pid = self.__get_pid(self.hwnd))

    @classmethod
    def find_instances(cls, name: str) -> list[AppProcess]:
        instances: list[AppProcess] = []
        for view in cls.__MANAGERS.view_collection.GetViewsByZOrder().iter(IApplicationView):
            if bool(view.GetShowInSwitchers()):
                if (instance := cls(view = view)).name() == name:
                    instances.append(instance)
        return instances

    def __get_pid(self, hWnd: int) -> int:
        pid = wintypes.DWORD()
        tid = self.__GetWindowThreadProcessId(hWnd, ctypes.byref(pid))
        if tid == 0:
            raise ctypes.WinError(ctypes.get_last_error())
        return pid.value

    def __init_win32_api_function_prototypes(self):
        user32 = ctypes.WinDLL('user32', use_last_error = True)

        # https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/winuser/nf-winuser-getwindowthreadprocessid
        # DWORD GetWindowThreadProcessId(
        #   [in]            HWND    hWnd,
        #   [out, optional] LPDWORD lpdwProcessId
        # );
        self.__GetWindowThreadProcessId = user32.GetWindowThreadProcessId
        self.__GetWindowThreadProcessId.argtypes = [wintypes.HWND, wintypes.LPDWORD]
        self.__GetWindowThreadProcessId.restype = wintypes.DWORD

        # https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/winuser/nf-winuser-getwindowtextw
        # int GetWindowTextW(
        #   [in]  HWND   hWnd,
        #   [out] LPWSTR lpString,
        #   [in]  int    nMaxCount
        # );
        self.__GetWindowText = user32.GetWindowTextW
        self.__GetWindowText.argtypes = [wintypes.HWND, wintypes.LPWSTR, wintypes.INT]
        self.__GetWindowText.restype = wintypes.BOOL

        # https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/winuser/nf-winuser-getwindowtextlengthw
        # int GetWindowTextLengthW(
        #   [in] HWND hWnd
        # );
        self.__GetWindowTextLength = user32.GetWindowTextLengthW
        self.__GetWindowTextLength.argtypes = [wintypes.HWND]
        self.__GetWindowTextLength.restype = wintypes.INT


if __name__ == '__main__':
    for process in AppProcess.find_instances(name = 'Spotify.exe'):
        print(process.caption)

Q: Running Windows 11 GUI Applications in Azure CI/CD Pipeline A:

Prepare your own machine and log in as a normal user. Then configure the agent to run as that normal user too and in user session. After that I believe the workflow will run fine for you. Just don’t run the agent as service under system session, as that creates enough problems due to the design of system session.
